name: Binary Spiders
description: Binary Spiders are species of spiders that live on Mars. These spiders weave their webs to defend themselves from enemies. To weave a web, spiders join in pairs. If the first spider in pair has $$$x$$$ legs, and the second spider has $$$y$$$ legs, then they weave a web with durability $$$x \oplus y$$$. Here, $$$\oplus$$$ means bitwise XOR. Binary Spiders live in large groups. You observe a group of $$$n$$$ spiders, and the $$$i$$$-th spider has $$$a_i$$$ legs. When the group is threatened, some of the spiders become defenders . Defenders are chosen in the following way. First, there must be at least two defenders. Second, any pair of defenders must be able to weave a web with durability at least $$$k$$$. Third, there must be as much defenders as possible. Scientists have researched the behaviour of Binary Spiders for a long time, and now they have a hypothesis that they can always choose the defenders in an optimal way, satisfying the conditions above. You need to verify this hypothesis on your group of spiders. So, you need to understand how many spiders must become defenders. You are not a Binary Spider, so you decided to use a computer to solve this problem.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 3\cdot10^5$$$, $$$0 \le k \le 2^{30} - 1$$$), the amount of spiders in the group and the minimal allowed durability of a web. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_i$$$ ($$$0 \le a_i \le 2^{30}-1$$$) — the number of legs the $$$i$$$-th spider has.
output_specification: In the first line, print a single integer $$$\ell$$$ ($$$2 \le \ell \le n$$$), the maximum possible amount of defenders. In the second line, print $$$\ell$$$ integers $$$b_i$$$, separated by a single space ($$$1 \le b_i \le n$$$) — indices of spiders that will become defenders. If there exists more than one way to choose the defenders, print any of them. Unfortunately, it may appear that it's impossible to choose the defenders. In this case, print a single integer $$$-1$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1625D — Binary Spiders [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
